intro.caption: Lesson 2-1 — statistical questions. Clip Squad is going live, and Dex wants to run the Q&A poll. Three reader gates and a rival showdown stand between the squad and a real stream.

balloons.t: We go live soon! We need a poll question that gives us real data from our fans.
I am recording! Please make it a good question this time.
Easy! My poll asks: How many cameras are in our studio? It uses numbers, so it's statistical!
Wait. Every fan would answer the exact same number. Where is the variety?

pages.caption: Having a number answer does NOT make a question statistical. A statistical question expects answers that vary.

balloons.t: Ask yourself: will different fans give different answers, or just one fixed fact?
Okay, Dex's last question flopped. Let's rewrite weak questions so the answers actually vary!
Ask about each viewer or each video instead of just one.
Look at our test polls. One has answers all over the place. The other is just the same number twelve times!
Twelve copies of the same number is a boring replay.
My poll asks how many trophies I won last year. It's a number, so it's statistical!
Nice try, Max. Let's pick real statistical questions for tonight's stream.
The comments are blowing up! Real statistical questions actually tell a story!

win.caption: A statistical question anticipates variability — different people or cases give different answers. A question with one fixed answer is not statistical, even when the answer is a number.

gates.title: Gate 1 · Sort the Questions
gates.prompt: Separate the real statistical questions from the one-answer traps.
hints: Conceptual: a statistical question expects answers that vary from person to person or case to case.
Procedural: ignore whether the answer is a number. Ask: will everyone give the same fixed answer, or different answers?

steps: Test: 'How many legs does a tripod have?' Everyone answers 3. One fixed answer, so NOT statistical.
Test: 'How many hours does each creator edit per week?' Some edit 2 hours, others 6 or 9. Answers vary, so it IS statistical.
Notice both answers are numbers — variability is what decides.
worked.q: Is 'How many days are in January?' a statistical question?

items.q: Which questions are statistical questions? Select all that apply.

options.t: How many minutes did each viewer watch our new clip?
How many subscribers does our channel have right now?
options.fb: That has numbers, but there is only ONE answer right now. No variability.

options.t: How many clips did each fan share this week?
How many seconds long is our intro video?
options.fb: That asks for one fixed length. Even with numbers, one answer is not statistical.

items.fbMiss: There are two statistical questions here — look for words like 'each viewer' and 'each fan'.
items.fbExtra: Check whether the question has only one fixed answer.

items.q: Dex says: 'My question How many cameras are in our studio? has a number answer, so it is statistical!' What is wrong with Dex's rule?

options.t: A question with a number is only statistical if the answers vary from case to case
Statistical questions cannot have number answers
options.fb: Many statistical questions have number answers, like watch minutes or ages.

options.t: Studio questions are never statistical
options.fb: You can ask statistical questions about a studio, like how many clips each camera filmed.

options.t: It is statistical because you can count the cameras
options.fb: Counting one fixed set gives one answer, not varied data.

gates.pass: Dex drops the camera-count question. Now the board only holds questions that actually vary.

gates.title: Gate 2 · Rewrite the Poll
gates.prompt: Turn one-answer questions into statistical questions for the channel.
hints: Conceptual: to make a question statistical, change it so it measures many people, videos, or trials.
Procedural: look for phrases like 'each video' or 'each viewer' that invite different answers.

steps: Weak question: 'How tall is Nova?' (One person, one fixed height.)
Keep the topic, add variety: 'How tall is each student in Nova's class?'
Now different students give different heights, so you must collect data.
worked.q: Rewrite 'How many views did our newest clip get?' to be statistical.
worked.a: How many views did each of our clips get?

items.q: Dex wrote: 'How many likes did our skate replay get?' How do you rewrite it into a statistical question?

options.t: How many likes did our skate replay get on Monday?
options.fb: That still asks about one video on one day — one fixed number.

options.t: How many likes did each of our last 10 videos get?
Did our skate replay get more than 50 likes?
options.fb: That is a yes-or-no question about one video, so it has one answer.

options.t: What is the total number of likes on our channel?
options.fb: A single total gives one number, not varied answers across videos.

items.q: Jaylen wants to ask: 'What time did our stream start?' Which rewrite adds variability?

options.t: What time does the stream start tomorrow?
options.fb: One stream has one start time — no variety.

options.t: How long did our stream last?
options.fb: One stream has one length — still one fixed answer.

options.t: How many minutes did each viewer stay on the stream?
Who clicked play first on the stream?
options.fb: That names one person, not a set of varied answers.

gates.pass: Two crisp rewrites! Both polls now ask about EACH video or EACH viewer.

gates.title: Gate 3 · Spot Variability
gates.prompt: Compare two test polls to see which one actually shows variability.
hints: Conceptual: variability means the collected values differ from one another.
Procedural: look at the list of answers. If every value is identical, there is zero variability.

steps: List X: 5, 5, 5, 5, 5. Only 1 distinct value appears — zero variability.
List Y: 2, 4, 2, 7, 5. Four distinct values appear (2, 4, 5, 7) — clear variability.
Variability shows up in the spread of different answers.

items.q: Poll A asked 12 fans how many videos they watched today: 1, 3, 2, 5, 1, 4, 2, 6, 3, 2, 4, 1. Poll B asked 12 fans how many wheels a standard skateboard has, and all 12 wrote 4. Which poll shows variability?

options.t: Poll A, because the answers differ from fan to fan
Poll B, because 12 fans answered it
options.fb: Asking 12 people the same fact still gives the exact same answer: 4.

options.t: Both polls, because both have number answers
options.fb: Numbers alone do not make variability. Look at whether the answers actually differ.

options.t: Neither poll, because 12 is too small
options.fb: Twelve fans is enough to see whether answers vary.

items.label: In Poll A (1, 3, 2, 5, 1, 4, 2, 6, 3, 2, 4, 1), how many DIFFERENT values appear?
items.aria: number of different values in Poll A

fb.msg: 12 is how many fans answered. Count how many different numbers appear: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
If only 1 value appeared, there would be no variability. List the unique numbers.

items.fbDefault: List the unique numbers in Poll A without repeating any, then count them.

gates.pass: Six distinct answers in Poll A vs one repeated 4 in Poll B. Variability spotted!

gates.title: Boss Gate · Pick the Stream Poll
gates.prompt: Max Maxwell is trying to sneak a fake statistical question onto the live stream. Shut it down and pick the real polls.
hints: Conceptual: a number answer does NOT make a question statistical. Ask whether the answers will vary.
Procedural: reject questions about one person, one video, or one fixed fact, and keep questions about 'each' fan or video.

steps: Check: 'How many gold buttons did Max buy?' — one count, one answer, NOT statistical.
Check: 'How many minutes did each subscriber watch Max's stream?' — varies by subscriber, statistical.
Pick only questions that invite a distribution of different answers.
worked.q: Is 'What year was the skate park built?' statistical?

items.q: Max's poll asks: 'How many trophies did Max win in last year's cup?' Max says it is statistical because the answer is a number. Is Max right?

options.t: Yes — any question answered with a number is statistical
options.fb: That is the number trap! One trophy count is one fixed fact.

options.t: No — it has one fixed answer, so there is no variability
Yes — because trophies are sports data
options.fb: Topic does not make a question statistical; variability does.

options.t: No — because you cannot count trophies
options.fb: You can count them, and you still get one single number.

items.q: Pick ALL the statistical questions for tonight's Clip Squad stream.

options.t: How many times did each fan replay Dex's wipeout?
How many seconds long is Dex's wipeout clip?
options.fb: One clip has one exact length — no variability.

options.t: Which Clip Squad stunt was each fan's favorite?
What year did Clip Squad launch its channel?
options.fb: The launch year is one fixed fact.

items.fbMiss: There are two statistical questions here — both ask about 'each fan'.
items.fbExtra: One fixed clip length or launch year does not vary.

items.q: Why is 'How many comments did each of our 8 new videos get?' better for the newsroom report than 'How many comments did our channel get in total?'

options.t: It shows variability across videos instead of hiding it in one total
The total is always smaller than each video's count
options.fb: The total is at least as big as any one video — that is not why.

options.t: Comments only count if you ask about 8 videos
options.fb: Any number of videos works; the key is comparing across videos.

options.t: A total is never a number
options.fb: A total is a number, just one fixed number with no spread.

gates.pass: Max's rigged poll is off the air, and Clip Squad's live Q&A hits a record turnout!

journal.heading: Lesson 2-1 — what the live poll taught us
rows: A question you answer by collecting data that are expected to vary across people, videos, or trials.
A question with one fixed answer — even if that answer is a number, like the number of cameras in the studio.
How much the collected answers differ from one another instead of all landing on the same value.
Rewriting 'our video' to 'each of our videos' turns a one-fact question into a statistical question.
journal.quote: "If everybody gives the exact same answer, you did not run a poll — you read a fact." — Blink

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 2-1 (Understand Statistical Questions) as one focused read. Whole-class on a projector, pairs on devices, or independent practice. It covers only this lesson: distinguishing statistical from non-statistical questions, spotting variability, and rewriting fixed-answer questions.
standards: Recognize a statistical question as one that anticipates variability in the data
